Nachträglich soll ich Euer Hochwohlgebohren auf des
Fürsten durchlaucht Befehl anliegende Charta
blanche zur Antwort an den H. von Rewen[?]
zusenden; dieselben mögten die Gewogen¬
heit haben, und sie nach dero Ansicht aus¬
fertigen laſsen. Auch den Auszug aus
einem Schreiben des B. R. Glenck lege ich hier
bey, wie es mir Sr. Durchlaucht befehlen
haben. Die Narrheit dieses Menschen, sein
immer reger aber um so unsinniger Specu¬
lations — Geist, sein Leichtsinn und seine
Frau Gemahlin haben ihn an den Randdes
Abgrundes geführt, an dem er wirklich
steht. Sowohl der Großmuth des Fürsten
als auch der Euer Hochwohlgebohren bleibt
es nun vorbehalten, ob Sie ihm noch ein
mal die Hand der Rettung reichen wollen
Sr. Durchlaucht sind hierzu bereit, und
fordern dieselben, zu gleicher Handlungs¬
weise hierdurch auf; und ich müßte dero
großmüthiges gerne vorgebendes Herz nicht
kennen, wenn Sie dem Wunsche des für¬
sten in dieser Hinsicht nicht entsprochen
wollten, wenn es irgend möglich ist.
Um dies zu bewirken bleibt es Euer
Hochwohlgebohren überlassen, durch
die Uebersendung des Schemas zum
Consens an Sr Durchlaucht, den p Glenck
endlich zum schweigen zu bringen.
Sr Durchl. wünschen es, auch und der
immerwärenden Klaglieder dieses
Mannes willen; die mit jedem Post
Tage anlangen. Schlägt der Glenck
die vielleicht nöthigen Bedingungen
Auszug, aus dem Schreiben des Glencks
d. d. 22ten Mrz 1806.
In dem Gedraenge worin mich das Wrąbczyner Güthern
und die Zahlungs-Ausflucht sezt, habe ich zum Ver¬
setzen, von Habseeligkeiten und zum Kleider
Verkaufen, zum Borgen mit wenigen Thalern
meine Zuflucht nehmen müßen. Mein abgedank¬
tes Gesinde, hat den Lärmen noch mehr verschrien
und da auch das Publicum in die Meinung ge¬
bracht wurde, daß ich außer Bedeutung bey
Euer Durchl. sey so erfolgte ein gänzlicher
Wlisd Credit auf mich meine zahlreichen Schuld¬
ner wurden laut und ich mußte tägtäglich
nur umher räumen nun zu leihen und die
gerichtlichen Klagen abwenden, und die
nöthigsten Haus-Bedürfnisse zu erborgen
suchen, da ich meine Besoldung für Schulden
Zahlungen eigentlich Proxenetica hingeben
mußte. So habe ich nach Wilhelmsruhe
gegen die Subtestation und einen niedri¬
gen Verkauf gerettet, das ich aus Pflicht für
die Menngen bis dahin, wohin es einen höhern
Werth erhalten wird, mit dem Verkauf
zögern muß, indem ich hier ein Glenck
voraussehen, wenn ich es noch eine Zeitlang
behaupten kann, und dazu gehört, daß ich
durch Vorzeigung des Consenses den Rybbeck
aus dem Kauf von Wrąbczyn bringe und
dis Gut einem bessern Mann überlassen
kann. Meine Familie bedarf diesen Schutz p
zu einem Arrangement abermals aus, wie es
bereits geschah, so bleibt freylich nichts übrig
als ihm in das Verderben vollen zu lassen,
was ihm sein Schwindel Geist zubereitete.
Mein grenzenloses Vertrauen in Euer
Hochwohlgebohren und ich darf sagen die
Gewogenheit, welche mir dieselben immer
bezeigten, und die mich immer mit wahrem
Stolz und Zuversicht in mich selbst beseelte
brachten diese Aeußerungen hervor,
und ich kann von denenselben hoffen, daß
Sie selbige nicht übel deuten werden.
Mit unbegrenzter Verehrung
Öhringen
d 10ten April
1806.
A Hahn

translation.en: 190 By way of supplement I am, on the command of His Serene Highness the Prince, to send Your Right Honourable the enclosed charta blanche for the reply to Mr von Rewen[uncertain: Rewen], which you may be pleased to have made out according to your own view of the matter. I also enclose herewith the extract from a letter of the mining councillor Glenck, as His Serene Highness has commanded me. The folly of this man, his ever-active but all the more senseless spirit of speculation, his frivolity and his lady wife have led him to the brink of the abyss, on which he truly stands. It now rests with the magnanimity both of the Prince and of Your Right Honourable whether you will once more extend to him the hand of rescue.

His Serene Highness is ready for this, and hereby calls upon you to act in the same manner; and I should have to be ignorant of your magnanimous and readily giving heart if you were not willing to comply with the Prince's wish in this respect, should it be in any way possible. In order to bring this about, it is left to Your Right Honourable to bring Glenck at last to silence by sending the draft of the consent to His Serene Highness. His Serene Highness desires it, also for the sake of this man's never-ceasing lamentations, which arrive with every post day. Should Glenck refuse the conditions that may be necessary

Extract from Glenck's letter

dated 22nd March 1806. In the straits in which the Wrąbczyn estates and the evasion of payment place me, I have had to take refuge in pawning my belongings, in selling clothes, and in borrowing small sums of a few thalers. My dismissed servants have cried the uproar abroad still further, and since the public too was brought to the opinion that I stood of no account with Your Serene Highness, there followed a complete [uncertain: Wlisd] of credit for me; my numerous creditors grew loud, and day after day I had only to go about [uncertain: räumen nun] to borrow and to avert the actions at law, and to seek to borrow the most necessary household requisites, since I had to give up my salary for the payment of debts, properly speaking as brokerage. Thus I have saved Wilhelmsruhe from the [uncertain: Subtestation] and from a low sale, so that out of duty towards my own people I must delay the sale until such time as it will fetch a higher

value, since I foresee here a [uncertain: Glenck] if I can hold out a while longer; and to that end it is necessary that, by producing the consent, I get Rybbeck out of the purchase of Wrąbczyn and can leave this estate to a better man. My family stands in need of this protection.

for an arrangement once again, as has already happened, then nothing will of course remain but to let him [uncertain: vollen] into the ruin which his giddy spirit has prepared for him. My boundless confidence in Your Right Honourable, and, I may say, the favour which you have always shown me, and which has always animated me with true pride and assurance in myself, have brought forth these utterances, and I may hope of you that you will not take them ill. With boundless veneration

Öhringen

the 10th of April

1806.

A Hahn

dated 22nd March 1806. In the straits in which the Wrąbczyn estates and the evasion of payment place me, I have had to take refuge in pawning my belongings, in selling clothes, and in borrowing small sums of a few thalers. My dismissed servants have cried the uproar abroad still further, and since the public too was brought to the opinion that I stood of no account with Your Serene Highness, there followed a complete [uncertain: Wlisd] of credit for me; my numerous creditors grew loud, and day after day I had only to go about [uncertain: räumen nun] to borrow and to avert the actions at law, and to seek to borrow the most necessary household requisites, since I had to give up my salary for the payment of debts, properly speaking as brokerage. Thus I have saved Wilhelmsruhe from the [uncertain: Subtestation] and from a low sale, so that out of duty towards my own people I must delay the sale until such time as it will fetch a higher

value, since I foresee here a [uncertain: Glenck] if I can hold out a while longer; and to that end it is necessary that, by producing the consent, I get Rybbeck out of the purchase of Wrąbczyn and can leave this estate to a better man. My family stands in need of this protection.

for an arrangement once again, as has already happened, then nothing will of course remain but to let him [uncertain: vollen] into the ruin which his giddy spirit has prepared for him. My boundless confidence in Your Right Honourable, and, I may say, the favour which you have always shown me, and which has always animated me with true pride and assurance in myself, have brought forth these utterances, and I may hope of you that you will not take them ill. With boundless veneration

Öhringen

the 10th of April

1806.

A Hahn
summary_en: On the Prince's instructions, Hahn sends a charta blanche and an extract from Glenck's letter of 22 March 1806. The Prince wants to rescue Glenck once more and calls on Triebenfeld to act in the same way and to send him the draft of the consent. If Glenck again rejects the conditions, he is to be left to his ruin. Glenck complains of hardship because of the Wrąbczyn estates, says he has saved Wilhelmsruh from forced sale, and wants to use the consent to get Rybbeck out of the purchase of Wrąbczyn.
summary_de: Hahn übersendet im Auftrag des Fürsten eine Charta blanche und einen Auszug aus Glencks Schreiben vom 22. März 1806. Der Fürst will Glenck noch einmal retten und fordert Triebenfeld auf, ebenso zu handeln und ihm das Schema zum Consens zu schicken. Lehnt Glenck die Bedingungen erneut ab, soll man ihn seinem Verderben überlassen. Glenck klagt über Not wegen der Wrąbczyner Güter, hat Wilhelmsruh vor der Subhastation gerettet und will mit dem Consens Rybbeck aus dem Kauf von Wrąbczyn bringen.

reading.notes: Hahn, the Prince's secretary, writes from Öhringen to Triebenfeld. On the Prince's orders he sends a blank signed sheet (charta blanche) for a reply to a H. von Rewen[?] (doubtful name) and an extract from Glenck's letter of 22 March 1806. Glenck is close to ruin. The Prince is ready to help him and asks Triebenfeld to do the same, by sending the Prince the draft (Schema) of the consent, so that Glenck's complaints stop. If Glenck refuses the conditions again, he is to be left to his ruin. In the extract, Glenck describes his distress over the Wrąbczyn estates. He has saved Wilhelmsruh from forced sale and wants to show the consent to get Rybbeck out of the Wrąbczyn purchase.
